subChunks.title: Dimensional Modelling — Fact Tables and Dimension Tables
subChunks.hookHtml: The data warehouse is where historical data is stored for analysis. Dimensional modelling — star schema and snowflake schema — is the standard way to organise it for fast analytical queries.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Fact tables

A fact table records events or transactions — one row per event, mostly foreign keys and numeric measures.

-- A quest completion fact:
fact_quest_completions(
  date_key      INT REFERENCES dim_date(date_key),
  apprentice_key INT REFERENCES dim_apprentice(apprentice_key),
  quest_key     INT REFERENCES dim_quest(quest_key),
  xp_earned     INT,
  score         DECIMAL(5,2),
  completion_time_seconds INT
)

Dimension tables

Dimension tables store descriptive attributes used for filtering and grouping.

dim_date(date_key, full_date, year, month, week, day_of_week, is_holiday)
dim_apprentice(apprentice_key, name, rank, mentor_name, cohort_year)
dim_quest(quest_key, title, difficulty, school, xp_reward, min_rank)

Star schema

One fact table surrounded by dimension tables — like a star. Denormalised dimension tables (all attributes in one table). Fast for analytics because joins are simple (fact → dimension).

Snowflake schema

Dimensions are normalised — split into sub-dimensions. dim_apprentice → dim_rank → dim_cohort. More normalised, saves some storage, but adds join complexity.

Surrogate keys

Warehouse dimensions use integer surrogate keys (date_key, apprentice_key) rather than natural keys. Surrogate keys are stable even when the natural key changes (e.g. apprentice name changes).

Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCD)

  • SCD Type 1 — overwrite: update the record in place (lose history)
  • SCD Type 2 — insert new row: keep the old row; add a new row with current values and a new surrogate key. Analysis can show what the dimension looked like at the time of each fact.

storyBeats.text: The analytics team wants to know: which mentor's apprentices complete the most hard quests? The answer spans three tables and two years of history.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: In a warehouse, you denormalise deliberately. The fact table holds numbers — what happened. Dimension tables hold context — who, what, when, where. A star schema joins them with one hop from fact to each dimension. Every analytical query is: which facts, grouped by which dimension attributes?

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Star schema design

Design a star schema for this reporting question: "What is the total XP earned per month, per rank tier, and per quest school for the past 2 years?". Identify the fact table and at least 2 dimension tables.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
Fact table: fact_xp_earnings
- date_key FK → dim_date
- apprentice_key FK → dim_apprentice
- quest_key FK → dim_quest
- xp_earned INT (the measure)
- completion_id INT (natural key from OLTP)

Dimension: dim_date
- date_key INT PK (surrogate)
- full_date DATE
- year INT
- month INT
- month_name TEXT
- quarter INT

Dimension: dim_apprentice
- apprentice_key INT PK (surrogate)
- apprentice_id INT (OLTP natural key)
- name TEXT
- rank TEXT
- rank_tier TEXT  -- APPRENTICE / JUNIOR / SENIOR / LEAD
- mentor_name TEXT (denormalised)
- valid_from DATE, valid_to DATE  -- SCD Type 2 to track rank changes

Dimension: dim_quest
- quest_key INT PK (surrogate)
- quest_id INT
- title TEXT
- school TEXT  -- Evocation / Divination / etc.
- difficulty TEXT
- xp_reward INT

The query:
SELECT d.year, d.month_name, a.rank_tier, q.school, SUM(f.xp_earned)
FROM fact_xp_earnings f
JOIN dim_date d ON f.date_key = d.date_key
JOIN dim_apprentice a ON f.apprentice_key = a.apprentice_key
JOIN dim_quest q ON f.quest_key = q.quest_key
WHERE d.year >= EXTRACT(YEAR FROM NOW()) - 2
GROUP BY d.year, d.month_name, a.rank_tier, q.school
ORDER BY d.year, d.month_name;
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Explain Slowly Changing Dimension Type 2. Describe how it would be implemented for an apprentice's rank changing from 'Apprentice' to 'Adept', and why it matters for historical reporting.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
SCD Type 2 maintains full history of dimension attribute changes by adding a new row when a change occurs, rather than overwriting.

Implementation for rank change:
Before: dim_apprentice row:
  (key=101, id=1, name='Alice', rank='Apprentice', valid_from='2024-01-01', valid_to=NULL, is_current=TRUE)

When Alice is promoted to Adept on 2024-06-15:
1. Close old row: UPDATE dim_apprentice SET valid_to='2024-06-15', is_current=FALSE WHERE key=101
2. Insert new row: (key=102, id=1, name='Alice', rank='Adept', valid_from='2024-06-15', valid_to=NULL, is_current=TRUE)

Why it matters: a fact completion in March 2024 references key=101 (rank=Apprentice). An analysis asking 'what rank was the apprentice when they completed this quest?' correctly returns 'Apprentice' — not their current rank 'Adept'. Without SCD2, all historical facts would appear to have been done by an 'Adept', destroying the historical accuracy of the analysis.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between a fact table and a dimension table in a data warehouse. Why are dimension tables intentionally denormalised in a star schema?

questions.prompt: In a star schema, what does a fact table contain?
options: Numeric measures (XP earned, revenue, count) and foreign keys to dimension tables — one row per event
Descriptive attributes like name, rank, and category
questions.answer: Numeric measures (XP earned, revenue, count) and foreign keys to dimension tables — one row per event
questions.explanation: Fact tables are narrow and long — many rows, mostly numeric measures and foreign keys. They record what happened (the fact). Dimension tables describe the context (who, what, when, where).

questions.prompt: Why does a star schema use surrogate integer keys for dimension tables instead of natural business keys?
options: Surrogate keys are stable even when natural key values change (e.g. a product name changes), and they are faster to join (integer vs string)
Surrogate keys are required by all analytical databases
Natural keys cannot be NULL, making surrogate keys necessary
Star schema does not support string columns in joins
questions.answer: Surrogate keys are stable even when natural key values change (e.g. a product name changes), and they are faster to join (integer vs string)
questions.explanation: Natural keys (email, product SKU, name) can change over time. Surrogate integer keys never change regardless of business changes. They also produce smaller, faster JOIN operations than string comparisons.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between star schema and snowflake schema?
options: Star: dimension tables are denormalised (flat); Snowflake: dimension tables are further normalised into sub-dimensions
Star: used for OLTP; Snowflake: used for OLAP
Star: has one fact table; Snowflake: has multiple fact tables
Star: slower queries; Snowflake: faster queries
questions.answer: Star: dimension tables are denormalised (flat); Snowflake: dimension tables are further normalised into sub-dimensions
questions.explanation: In a star schema, dim_product contains product, category, and subcategory all in one table. In a snowflake, dim_product references dim_category which references dim_subcategory. Star schema is simpler to query; snowflake saves some storage but adds join complexity.

questions.prompt: An analyst needs to know what rank an apprentice held when they completed each quest (not their current rank). Which SCD type supports this?
options: SCD Type 2 — keeps a full history of dimension changes with valid_from/valid_to dates, allowing point-in-time lookups
SCD Type 1 — overwrites the current value
No SCD is needed — rank never changes
A separate audit table must be used
questions.answer: SCD Type 2 — keeps a full history of dimension changes with valid_from/valid_to dates, allowing point-in-time lookups
questions.explanation: SCD Type 2 preserves the state of a dimension at each point in time. Each fact record links to the dimension surrogate key that was current at the time of the event — enabling correct historical analysis even after the dimension changes.
